title: Styles of turban
hook: many styles, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla

segments.voice: Yesterday, caring for kesh: washing, combing and covering, every morning. Your line was daily care. What did you give a few slow minutes to? Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

Stand at the door of a big gurdwara on a festival morning and watch the heads come in. A neat, pointed turban in deep navy. A rounded one in bright saffron. A small cloth knotted on a boy's head. A tall, wound turban in dark blue, rising high, with a steel emblem fixed at the front. Pink at a wedding. White on an older man. Patterned cloth on a young woman. Same faith, same hall, same Guru at the front. Yesterday we ended with the covering; today we look at the covering itself, and how many shapes one idea can take.
screen: `HEADS AT THE GURDWARA DOOR.` → `NAVY, SAFFRON, WHITE, PINK.` → `ONE IDEA, MANY SHAPES.`

segments.voice: Begin with the everyday one. In Punjabi it's often just called the pagg, and its formal name is dastar. A long strip of cloth, folded and wound around the head in layers, finished neatly. Different families and regions tie it differently: one comes to a sharp peak at the front, another is rounder and softer, and people often learn the style of their father, an uncle or a friend. Next, the smaller coverings. A patka is a square of cloth tied over the hair knot, often worn by children before they learn the full turban, and by some people for sport. A keski is a shorter turban, worn by some under a larger one and by some, including some Sikh women who wear a turban, on its own. Then the tall one. The dumalla is wound high and full, sometimes with a steel emblem or small weapons tucked into it. It is closely tied to the Nihangs, the Sikh order known for keeping the old martial dress, and others wear it too. Color is mostly choice. Some match a shirt; some wear saffron or blue on festival days; some wear one color for years. Here's what joins them all. Earlier on this path, the code asked the turban of Sikh men and left it open to women, and our line was crowned. A crown can be tall or neat, bright or plain, and still be a crown. And that brings us to the end of the week: Patna and Hazur Sahib, the Sarbat Khalsa, the old rehatnamas, why a written code, caring for kesh, and now the turban itself. Many styles, one crown.
screen: `THE PAGG, OR DASTAR.` · `PATKA AND KESKI.` · `THE TALL DUMALLA.` · `TALL OR NEAT, STILL A CROWN.` · then, large: `MANY STYLES, ONE CROWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at different turban styles. If you can, look at a few pictures now, or bring to mind the turbans you've seen on a street, on a screen, at a gurdwara. Settle, and breathe. Notice each one without judging it: the shape, the color, the care in the folds. Then notice the person under it. Somebody wound that cloth this morning, layer by layer, with their own hands. Stay with that picture of the work, and the care in it, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Styles of turban. Many ways to tie it, from the everyday pagg to the tall dumalla, each one the same crown. Today's word.
Your line: many styles, one crown. Today, when you see someone in a turban, notice the style and the care, and let it be a crown. Day one thousand two hundred eighty-eight.

notes: Descriptions of the pagg/dastar, patka, keski and dumalla are general; please confirm, especially that a keski is worn alone by some, including Sikh women who wear a turban, and the description of the Nihangs as 'the Sikh order known for keeping the old martial dress'.
Colors (saffron or blue on festival days, pink at weddings, white on an older man) are illustrative, not rules; please confirm none is misleading.
